column4: The section joins being overlooked with wanting to be seen; this ayah opens a scene with a person turning away, and the continuation reveals that his attention had gone to the self-sufficient while a vulnerable visitor waited.
This continuation identifies the arriving person as blind; the section's missed orphan and poor similarly stand at the edge of another's attention, though this ayah's visitor is not said to be poor.
The section says the person looked past can contain an unseen inner life; this continuation asks whether the blind visitor might become purified, making his potential a reason not to dismiss him.
The same visitor might remember and benefit from a reminder; this adds the possible spiritual benefit that the neglecting gaze in the section fails to see.

The section's vulnerable people are passed over while its actors seek notice; the next figure in this scene is one who considers himself self-sufficient, the socially powerful person whose attention draws the gaze.
This ayah says attention is directed toward that self-sufficient figure; it identifies where the gaze went in the scene of overlooking the blind visitor.

The passage bounds the preacher's responsibility by saying he is not accountable if the self-sufficient man refuses purification; that distinction helps keep the section's failure of care separate from the recipient's response.
The passage turns to another arrival, one who comes striving; this keeps the focus on the person who actively seeks attention after the well-positioned figure received it.
This arriving person fears God; the detail makes his inward seriousness visible in the very scene where the gaze is diverted from him.
The ayah says attention is diverted from the striving, God-fearing arrival; this is the same specific failure of sight and attention developed by the section's overlooked vulnerable people.

The section says needy people are overlooked as faint; this verse describes poor people whose restraint makes the uninformed think they are self-sufficient, though they can be recognized by their signs and do not persistently ask.
The section depicts a hand driving the vulnerable away; this command forbids driving away people who call on their Lord morning and evening, protecting their place in the gathering.

This command says to stay with those who call on their Lord and not let one's eyes pass beyond them for worldly adornment; it meets the section's eyes-for-people image with a direct boundary on whom to keep in view.
The section says an orphan has lost a protective circle; this verse makes the guardian's concrete duty to deliver orphans' property and not consume it part of that protection.
Continuing the orphan-care rules, this ayah requires testing until maturity and handing over property when judgment is sound; it specifies how a guardian preserves what belongs to the child.
Alongside its command for just measure, this ayah forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best way until maturity, joining protection of the vulnerable to a measured due.

This repeated command likewise forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best way until maturity; it makes the lost-guardian image concrete as a continuing duty to safeguard the child's resources.

The section's shelter image meets the story of a wall built for two orphans so their treasure remains protected until they mature; the verse makes hidden, future provision a reason to preserve a place for children.
The section reads al-ma'un as zakah and a due; this verse assigns zakah among the poor, needy, debtors, and other named recipients, specifying how a share reaches people who need it.
The section's dictionary gloss includes a tight-handed person; this command pictures the hand chained to the neck and forbids that restraint, setting generosity between withholding and waste.

The section says its actors want not to be overlooked while denying the Day; after such people forget their meeting with that Day, this verse says they will be forgotten and their refuge is the Fire, a direct reversal of their wish to remain seen.
The section shows people withholding small help; this verse tells people of means not to swear off giving to relatives, the needy, and migrants, and urges pardon, directly reversing the closed hand.

The section gathers care for vulnerable people, prayer, and zakah into a broken circle; this covenant joins worship, care for orphans and poor people, good speech, prayer, and zakah, then notes that most turned away.
This command joins worship of God with goodness to orphans and needy people, then condemns arrogant self-display; it gathers the section's social duties and outward-looking failure in one address.

The chiefs reject Noah's followers as the lowest people and say they see no distinction in them; this scene explicitly stages the social gaze that discounts the lowly whom the section says are passed over.
Noah answers that he will not drive away the believers; the verse directly reverses the section's pushing away of the vulnerable and says those believers will meet their Lord.
Noah asks who would protect him from God if he drove the believers away; this continuation ties refusal to expel the lowly to the protection image developed around the orphan.
Noah refuses to declare that those whom people's eyes scorn will receive no good from God; this directly challenges the section's way of overlooking the dim and vulnerable.
